'''''Bambusa tulda''''', or '''Indian timber bamboo''' (alternatively '''spineless Indian bamboo''' or '''Bengal bamboo'''<ref>[https://www.monaconatureencyclopedia.com/bambusa-tulda-2/ Monaco Nature Encyclopedia]</ref>), is considered to be one of the most useful of [[bamboo]] species. It is native to the [[Indian subcontinent]], [[Indochina]], [[Tibet]], and [[Yunnan]], and naturalized in [[Iraq]], [[Puerto Rico]], and parts of [[South America]].<ref name=f>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=399088 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=103452 Flora of China Vol. 22 Page 21, <big>俯竹</big> fu zhu, ''Bambusa tulda'' Roxburgh, Fl. ''B. tulda'' is used extensively by the [[paper pulp]] industry in India. It can grow to a height of 15 m and a thickness of 8 cm. The single most important fact about Bambusa tulda is its incredible tensile strength; up to 60,000 pounds (27,000 Kg) per square inch. <ref>{{cite book |date=1948 |last=McClure |first=Floyd A. |title=U.S.D.A yearbook of Agriculture-Grasses-"Bamboos for Farm and Home" |location=Washington, DC |publisher=U.S. Dept. of Agriculture |page=738}}</ref> It is commonly found in southeastern Asia.<ref>[http://www.bamboo-oz.com.au/species/B_tulda.html Bambusa tulda] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070829111428/http://bamboo-oz.com.au/species/B_tulda.html |date=2007-08-29 }}, OzBamboo; ''Retrieved: 2007-12-19''</ref>

==Habit==
It is a tall, dull green colored bamboo species with greyish green when mature. It is composed of few closely growing culms. It reaches a height of 6–23 m.

==Appearance==
Young culms are green, which become greyish green when mature and brown when drying. Young shoots are yellowish green in color with a powdery top. Culms are covered with white blooms. A band of white hairs occurs above the nodes. Branching occurs from the base to top. Aerial roots reach up to few nodes above. Internode length is 30–60 cm, and diameter is 0.8–1.2 cm. Culm walls are very thick. Nodes are prominent.

Culm sheaths are triangular with a conical blade, and straw-colored. The sheath proper is asymmetrical and 15–32 cm in length and 25–34 cm wide. Blade length is 5–10 cm. Auricles are unequal where the large one is rounded and situated on the side of the blade. The upper surface of the sheath is covered with blackish-brown hairs. The lower surface of the sheath is not hairy. Sheaths fall off early.
